title: I went to Agra yesterday — and the word that points both ways
title_target: कल मैं आगरा गई — kal maiⁿ aagraa gaii
goal: Talk about what has happened, and see why one and the same word can mean "yesterday" and "tomorrow" without confusing anyone.
bekal: forming the past of verbs without an object

dialogs.title: संवाद — Back from Agra
dialogs.intro: Ani has just come back from Agra. In line ten she asks something that may have puzzled you since Unit 9, and Priya's answer is the key to the whole Hindi time system.

lines.speaker: प्रिया:
lines.id: Wow! Did you see the Taj Mahal?

lines.speaker: प्रिया:
lines.id: How did you go? By train?

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.id: Yes, by train. I left at six in the morning.
lines.literal: ji — yes, train — by. morning — six — o'clock — set-out(fem.).

lines.speaker: प्रिया:
lines.id: And when did you get back?

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.id: In the evening. I was exhausted.
lines.literal: evening — at. very — tired — became(fem.) — was.

lines.speaker: प्रिया:
lines.id: Where are you off to tomorrow?

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.id: Wait — is that "kal" yesterday or tomorrow?
lines.literal: wait — "kal" — gone-by — kal — or — coming(obl.) — that — kal?

lines.speaker: प्रिया:
lines.id: (laughing) Look at the verb! "thiin" means yesterday, "ja rahi hain" means tomorrow.
lines.literal: (laughing — while) verb — look! "were" — gone-by — kal, "go — -ing — are" — coming — that — kal.

notes: **The past of होना: था · थी · थे · थीं.** *मैं ठीक **था*** (male), *मैं ठीक **थी*** (female), *हम ठीक **थे***, *वे ठीक **थे/थीं***. ⚠️ **थीं** is used for plural women **and** for a woman you respect — that's why Priya says *आप कहाँ **थीं***? to Ani alone.

**The past of verbs without an object: stem + आ · ई · ए · ईं.** जाना → गया · गई · गए · गईं. आना → आया · आई · आए · आईं. निकलना → निकला · निकली. सोना → सोया · सोई. ⚠️ The form follows the **subject**, just like the habitual in Unit 4. There's no second part like हूँ/है — the verb stands alone.

**Irregular past forms you must learn.** जाना → **गया** (not *जाया*), होना → **हुआ**, करना → **किया**, देना → **दिया**, लेना → **लिया**, पीना → **पिया**. The first is the most important and most frequent: *मैं गई*, *वे गए*, *वह गया*.

**गई थी — why two past words in a row?** *मैं गई* = I went. *मैं गई **थी*** = I had gone, before something else. In everyday speech, Indians often use the second form for yesterday's events without any special meaning. You don't need to tell them apart carefully yet; use the short form, and recognize the long one when you hear it.

⚠️ **Here's the answer: कल means "yesterday" AND "tomorrow", and the verb decides.** *कल मैं **गई*** (yesterday I went) versus *कल मैं **जाऊँगी*** (tomorrow I will go). The same goes for **परसों** (the day after tomorrow / the day before yesterday) and **नरसों** (three days from today, in either direction). Hindi names the **distance** from today and leaves the **direction** to the verb — economical, and never confusing to its own speakers.

**थक गई — two verbs again, and the second means "became, ended up".** *थकना* = to tire; *थक जाना* = to get tired, be worn out. Pairs like this are very common: **सो जाना** (fall asleep), **भूल जाना** (forget), **आ जाना** (turn up, arrive), **समझ जाना** (get it — the *समझ गई* you've been using since Unit 9). ⚠️ The second verb adds no new meaning; it adds a sense of "done, fully happened".

⚠️ **Line three of the dialogue hides something.** *ताजमहल देखा?* is really short for *आप**ने** ताजमहल देखा?* — with a ने you haven't learned yet. The reason: देखना has an **object** (the Taj Mahal), and verbs with objects behave completely differently in the past. That's the next unit, and it's the most unfamiliar part of Hindi for English speakers. For now, just note that every example in this unit — जाना, आना, निकलना, सोना, थकना — has **no object**.

after: ⚠️ Notice that **रहा · रही · रहे** in the last row is the same word as the "-ing" marker in Unit 11. That's no accident — the marker comes from the past of रहना. Context tells them apart: *वह वहाँ रहा* (he stayed there) versus *वह जा रहा है* (he is going).

rows: I left at six in the morning.
In the evening I came back.

after: **मज़ा आया** is the most natural way to say "it was fun" — literally "enjoyment came". Once again, a structure where the feeling happens to the person rather than being owned by them: *मुझे बहुत मज़ा आया*.

sections.title: Past time, and how to say it

blocks.text: Past time expressions go at the start of the sentence, like any other time expression. Only one thing to watch: the noun goes into the oblique form when a postposition follows.

head: हिंदी
Pronunciation
Meaning
rows: at that time, at that moment

blocks.title: Five questions about the past you'll hear
items: **आप कब आईं?** — When did you arrive? (to a woman)
**आप कितने दिन थे?** — How many days were you there? (to a man)
**कैसा रहा?** — How was it? (literally "how did it stay" — the question asked most often after a trip)
**कहाँ कहाँ गईं?** — Where all did you go? (remember the doubled question word from Unit 5)

blocks.text: A note on Ani's closing line — **आपकी भाषा चालाक है**. **चालाक** really does mean "sneaky, crafty", and here it's used as a joking compliment. ⚠️ Be careful using it about people: calling someone *चालाक* in front of others sounds like an accusation, not praise. To praise someone's intelligence, use **होशियार** (*ho-shi-yaar*) or **तेज़** (*tez*) — the word you met in Unit 7 when Priya praised Ani.

exercises.prompt: Fill in था, थी, थे or थीं.
Put the words in the right order.
Translate into Hindi. Assume you are a woman.
items: I left at six in the morning.
In the evening I came back.

answers: मैं गई। — वह आया। — हम पहुँचे। — वे सोए। — मैं थकी।
कल मैं आगरा गई। — बहुत भीड़ थी। — मैं सुबह छह बजे निकली। — बहुत मज़ा आया। — कल आप कहाँ थीं?
कल मैं घर पर थी। — मैं आगरा गई। — मैं सुबह छह बजे निकली। — मौसम अच्छा था। — रात को मैं वापस आई। — मैं थक गई थी।
